questions.prompt: In a backtracking function, `path.append(x)` is followed by the recursive call and then `path.pop()`. What is the `pop()` for?

choices.text: It frees memory so the recursion doesn't run out of space
It removes the finished answer from the results
It undoes the choice, so the next branch starts from the same state
It stops the recursion from going deeper

questions.explanation: Backtracking shares one `path` list across the whole search. After exploring everything that follows choosing `x`, `pop()` un-chooses it, so the sibling branch (not choosing `x`, or choosing the next candidate) sees `path` exactly as it was. The results list is separate and isn't touched, and the depth is limited by the base case, not by `pop()`.

questions.prompt:
This Subsets solution records answers with `res.append(path)` instead of `res.append(path[:])`. What does it return for `[1, 2, 3]`?

```python
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def bt(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path)
            return
        path.append(nums[i]); bt(i + 1)
        path.pop(); bt(i + 1)
    bt(0)
    return res
```

choices.text: The 8 correct subsets
A list of 8 empty lists
It raises `RecursionError`

questions.explanation: `res.append(path)` stores a reference to the one shared list, not a snapshot of it. All 8 entries are the same object, and by the time the search ends every `append` has been matched by a `pop`, so that object is empty. Append a copy (`path[:]` or `list(path)`) to record what the path holds at that moment.

questions.prompt: Explain the choose, explore, un-choose template for backtracking, and why you must record a copy of the path rather than the path itself.

model_answer.summary: Each call makes a choice by changing shared state, recurses on the smaller problem, then undoes the choice so the next option starts clean; because the state is one shared list, recording it needs a copy.
key_points: Choose: add a candidate to the path (and mark it used if the problem needs that)
Explore: recurse on what is left of the problem, with a base case that records a complete answer
Un-choose: pop the candidate (and unmark it), so the next sibling branch starts from the same state
The path is one list mutated throughout the search, so storing it stores a reference that later changes
Record `path[:]` (a copy); otherwise every recorded answer is the same list, which ends up empty

questions.explanation: Sharing one list and undoing changes is what makes backtracking cheap: no copying on the way down. The price is that the list's contents are only right at the moment you reach a base case, so that is when you take a snapshot.

questions.prompt: Subsets of `[1, 2, 3]` builds a recursion tree where each level decides whether to include one element. How deep is the tree, and how many leaves does it have?

choices.text: Depth 3 and 6 leaves
Depth 8 and 3 leaves
Depth 2 and 7 leaves
Depth 3 and 8 leaves

questions.explanation: There is one level per element, so 3 decisions from root to leaf. Each decision splits in two (include or exclude), so there are 2³ = 8 leaves, one per subset, from `[]` to `[1, 2, 3]`. 6 is the number of permutations of three items, and 7 forgets the empty subset.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of generating all subsets of n distinct numbers, counting the cost of copying each subset into the result?

choices.text: O(n × 2ⁿ)
O(2ⁿ)
O(n!)
O(n²)

questions.explanation: There are 2ⁿ subsets, and copying each one into the result costs up to n, so the total is O(n × 2ⁿ). Leaving out the copy gives O(2ⁿ), which undercounts. O(n!) is the number of orderings, which subsets don't care about.

questions.prompt: Describe the recursion tree for Subsets of `[1, 2, 3]` when each call first includes the next element and then excludes it. What is at each level, and in what order are the subsets recorded?

model_answer.summary: Level i decides whether to include element i, giving a binary tree of depth 3 with 8 leaves, recorded in the order [1,2,3], [1,2], [1,3], [1], [2,3], [2], [3], [].
key_points: The root has an empty path; level 1 decides 1, level 2 decides 2, level 3 decides 3
Every node has two children, include or exclude, so the tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes
Each of the 8 leaves is one subset, recorded at the base case when all 3 elements are decided

questions.explanation: Drawing the tree makes the complexity visible: 2ⁿ leaves, n levels. It also shows why the include-or-exclude version never produces a duplicate: each leaf is a different set of yes-or-no answers.

questions.prompt: In Combination Sum, after choosing `candidates[i]` you recurse with the same start index `i`, not `i + 1`. Why?

choices.text: So the combinations come out sorted
Because the same number may be used an unlimited number of times
To skip candidates that are larger than the target
Because `i + 1` could run past the end of the list

questions.explanation: The problem lets you reuse a candidate any number of times, so after picking `candidates[i]` you may pick it again. Recursing with `i + 1` allows each number once: for `[2, 3, 6, 7]` and target 7 it finds only `[7]` and misses `[2, 2, 3]`. The index never moving backwards is what prevents duplicate orderings.

questions.prompt: A Combination Sum solution loops over every candidate from index 0 in every call, instead of from a start index. What does it return for `candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7]` and `target = 7`?

choices.text: Nothing, because it recurses forever

questions.explanation: Starting from index 0 every time lets the search pick 3 after 2 and also 2 after 3, so the same combination appears once per ordering. The problem counts combinations as different only if the counts differ, so these are duplicates. It doesn't recurse forever, because every candidate is at least 2 and the remaining target keeps shrinking.

questions.prompt: Explain how a Combination Sum backtracking solution avoids duplicate combinations, allows reuse, and knows when to stop.

model_answer.summary: Pass a start index so candidates are only chosen in index order, recurse with the same index to allow reuse, and stop a branch when the remaining target reaches zero (record it) or goes below zero (abandon it).
key_points: A start index means each call only picks candidates at or after it, so each combination is built in one order and found once
After choosing `candidates[i]`, recurse with `i` (not `i + 1`) so the same number can be chosen again
When the remaining target is 0, record a copy of the path
When the remaining target is below 0, or no candidates are left, abandon the branch
Every candidate is at least 2, so the remaining target strictly shrinks and the recursion always ends

questions.explanation: Duplicates come from order, and the start index removes order from the search by only moving forwards through the candidates. Pruning on the remaining target keeps the tree small; sorting the candidates first lets you stop the loop as soon as one candidate is bigger than what remains.

questions.prompt: Subsets uses a start index, but Permutations usually keeps a `used` array (or set) instead. Why?

choices.text: Order matters, so any unused element may come next, including earlier ones
Permutations may reuse an element, and `used` counts how many times
A start index would be slower to update than a `used` array
The input to Permutations may contain duplicates, which `used` filters out

questions.explanation: `[2, 1, 3]` and `[1, 2, 3]` are different permutations, so after choosing 2 the search must still be allowed to choose 1, which a forward-only start index would forbid. What it must not do is reuse an element already in the path, and `used` tracks exactly that. The problem says the integers are distinct.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of generating all permutations of n distinct numbers, counting the cost of copying each one into the result?

choices.text: O(2ⁿ)
O(n²)
O(n × n!)
O(nⁿ)

questions.explanation: There are n choices for the first position, n − 1 for the second, and so on, giving n! permutations; copying each costs n, so O(n × n!). For `[1, 2, 3]` that is 6 permutations. O(2ⁿ) counts subsets, and O(nⁿ) would allow an element to repeat.
